work.title: Plato, Crito
work.notes: Plato's dramatic representation of Socrates in prison. Keep Plato's authorship explicit and distinguish the argument against retaliation from broader, contested interpretations of obedience to law.

passages.translationText: Socr. Neither ought one who is injured to return the injury, as the multitude think, since it is on no account right to act unjustly. Cri. It appears not. Socr. What, then? Is it right to do evil, Crito, or not? Cri. Surely it is not right, Socrates. Socr. But what? To do evil in return when one has been evil-entreated, is that right, or not? Cri. By no means. Socr. For to do evil to men differs in no respect from committing injustice. Cri. You say truly. Socr. It is not right, therefore, to return an injury, or to do evil to any man, however one may have suffered from him.
passages.interpretiveNote: The argument rejects injustice and retaliation even after suffering wrong. It does not by itself settle every question of civil disobedience, political obligation, self-defence, or protection of others.
